item.title: A Configurational Approach to Investigating the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Self‐Regulated Learning From Needs Satisfaction, Learning Environments and Perceived Affordances
item.description:
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
ABSTRACT Background Integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools into self‐regulated learning (SRL) is complex and multifaceted. Configurational approaches are based on the concept that combinations (or configurations) of causally relevant factors should be connected to the desired outcome. Objectives Self‐determination theory (SDT), the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) and perceived affordances focus on basic needs, technology adoptions and technological designs, respectively. Taking a configurational approach, this study investigates how the combinations of SDT, UTAUT and perceived affordances affect SRL with AI. Methods We employed fuzzy‐set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to uncover the complex interplay of factors that facilitate effective SRL. Data from 248 students reveal that a combination of autonomy satisfaction, relatedness satisfaction and performance expectancy is the most influential factor affecting the use of AI in SRL. Results and Conclusions Our results suggest that both innate psychological needs and external learning environments should be considered together for understanding the adoption of AI in SRL. They also further highlight the critical role of perceived affordances as mediators and moderators, enhancing the relationships between innate psychological needs and external learning environments. This integrative approach provides valuable insights into the design and implementation of AI‐supported SRL environments. We recommend designing the environments to foster autonomy and relatedness while also ensuring ease of use for learners.

item.title: The longitudinal relationships among AI-assisted music classroom engagement, flow experience, and musical emotional intelligence: a parallel-process latent growth modeling study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Although artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into music education, limited research has examined how students’ classroom engagement, flow experience, and emotional intelligence develop together over time. This study investigated the longitudinal relationships among these three psychological constructs in AI-assisted music classrooms, with particular attention to their developmental trajectories and the indirect association involving changes in flow experience. Methods A five-wave longitudinal survey was conducted among 850 undergraduate music students from four Chinese universities, with 718 participants retained at the final measurement. AI-assisted music classroom engagement, flow experience, and self-perceived emotional intelligence in musical learning contexts were assessed at each wave. Longitudinal measurement invariance was examined, and parallel-process latent growth modeling was employed to investigate developmental trajectories and associations among growth factors. Indirect effects were evaluated using 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results Classroom engagement (slope = 0.044), flow experience (slope = 0.051), and emotional intelligence (slope = 0.046) exhibited significant positive growth over time (all p < 0.001), with significant individual differences in growth rates. The growth rate of classroom engagement was positively associated with that of flow experience ( r = 0.39), while the growth rate of flow experience was positively associated with that of emotional intelligence ( r = 0.40). Furthermore, a significant indirect association between engagement growth and emotional intelligence growth was observed through flow growth (indirect effect = 0.120, 95% bootstrap CI [0.064, 0.205]). This association remained significant in additional robustness analyses. Conclusion The findings reveal interconnected developmental trajectories of classroom engagement, flow experience, and self-perceived emotional intelligence in AI-assisted music learning contexts. Growth in flow experience emerged as a significant statistical link between changes in classroom engagement and emotional intelligence. These findings extend research on the longitudinal associations among engagement, flow, and emotional functioning in technology-supported music education, while highlighting the need for further research to establish the temporal and causal mechanisms underlying these relationships.

item.title: From chatbot to language-learning partner: learner–LLM configuration, affordances, and regulatory demands in foreign language learning
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as flexible resources for self-directed foreign-language learning, yet limited research explains how learners configure these systems as pedagogical partners. This study examined pedagogical role construction, modality–pedagogy alignment, affordance realization, breakdowns, and regulatory demands in learner–LLM interaction. Using a retrospective observational computational content-analysis design, 117 first-person public posts and comments, representing 80 pseudonymous participants, were analyzed from seven public forums and X. Structured multi-label coding and quantitative analyses identified eight pedagogical roles and examined relationships among interaction modalities, learning activities, perceived affordances, and breakdowns. Results showed that learners reported configuring LLMs as multifunctional pedagogical partners, most prominently as interlocutors, while 65.8% of accounts involved multiple roles. Voice interaction was significantly associated with conversation and pronunciation, whereas text was associated with vocabulary learning, supporting modality–pedagogy alignment. More orchestrated learning configurations were associated with greater perceived benefits, particularly personalization and convenience, although an apparent difference in activity breadth was substantially attenuated once the activities used to define orchestration were excluded from the count. However, 43.6% of accounts reported concerns, revealing function-specific breakdowns involving accuracy/language reliability, access/privacy/system constraints, pedagogical sustainability, interaction/continuity, and voice/technical reliability. The findings support an empirically informed framework conceptualizing learner–LLM interaction as an AI-mediated regulatory process involving role construction, modality and activity configuration, affordance realization, monitoring, breakdown detection, and regulatory demand. Psychological self-regulation and objective proficiency gains were not directly measured.

item.title: Priority structure and configurational pathways of professional role adaptation among university moral education teachers in the era of generative artificial intelligence
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
The continuing integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping the professional roles of university moral education teachers. Drawing on the theory of work role transitions and structured rating survey data from 70 university moral education teachers in China, this study combines the group analytic hierarchy process (group AHP) with fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to examine the relative priority of conditions for professional role adaptation and their combinational relationships. The results show that teacher identity and institutional resource support both have relatively high subjective priority, but their configurational patterns in professional role adaptation differ: teacher identity is present in both pathways associated with high professional role adaptation, whereas GenAI ethical discernment is specified in only one of them. Institutional resource support is configured differently depending on the combination of professional competence and GenAI-related role strain, indicating that its subjective priority does not imply that it is indispensable in every context of high professional role adaptation. Further findings indicate that higher levels of professional role adaptation are associated with combinations featuring relatively sufficient GenAI pedagogical competence, teacher identity, and institutional resource support, but may also occur in contexts with relatively insufficient GenAI pedagogical competence and institutional resource support, high GenAI ethical discernment, and low GenAI-related role strain. This suggests that professional role adaptation among moral education teachers in the GenAI context is not a simple accumulation of the sufficiency of individual resources, but an adaptation state characterized by differentiated configurational relationships among professional identity, ethical judgment, practical competence, and organizational context. The study reveals differences between teachers’ subjective judgments of the importance of conditions for professional role adaptation and the specific configurational relationships among these conditions, providing empirical evidence for understanding the continuity of teachers’ professional mission, adjustments to boundaries of responsibility, and the contextual nature of professional role adaptation during technological change.

item.title: Perceived and demonstrated generative AI literacy in engineering problem solving: the role of verification behavior
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly used in engineering education, but self-reported literacy may not establish whether students can evaluate its outputs. The distinction between perceived competence and performance on engineering-specific AI scenarios remains insufficiently examined. This study investigated their correspondence and whether reported verification frequency statistically accounted for the association between demonstrated literacy and engineering task performance. Methods A cross-sectional online survey and assessment involved 1,206 mechanical engineering students at three Chinese universities. Measures comprised a 20-item perceived literacy questionnaire, a 12-item scenario test, an eight-item verification frequency scale, and two engineering tasks. Mediation and moderated mediation models controlled gender, year of study, AI use, AI course experience, and university fixed effects. Results Perceived and demonstrated literacy were modestly correlated, r = 0.265, 95% confidence interval [0.212, 0.317]. Demonstrated literacy was associated with verification frequency, b = 0.065, and the adjusted indirect association with engineering performance was 0.124, 95% bootstrap confidence interval [0.096, 0.154]. A small negative interaction suggested a weaker verification-performance association at higher perceived literacy, but its practical importance remains uncertain. A reverse-order model also produced a nonzero indirect association. Discussion The findings support assessing self-perception and scenario performance separately and investigating the quality of verification. Because the assessment was unproctored, the scores do not establish unaided competence; the cross-sectional associations do not establish a causal verification mechanism.

item.title: Breaking career boundaries in the AI era: how AI literacy relates to university students’ perceived employability through future work self salience and boundaryless career mindset
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in learning and work, understanding its relevance to students’ career development is increasingly important. Drawing on a career construction perspective and boundaryless career theory, this study examined associations among self-reported AI literacy, future work self salience, boundaryless career mindset, and perceived employability. Methods Cross-sectional questionnaire data were collected from 1,945 university students in China. Confirmatory factor analysis and full latent-variable structural equation modeling were conducted. Specific and theoretically ordered indirect associations were evaluated using bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals. Results Self-reported AI literacy was positively associated with perceived employability, with positive specific indirect associations through future work self salience and boundaryless career mindset. A theoretically ordered indirect association involving both constructs was also significant. However, an alternative model reversing their ordering yielded equivalent global fit, indicating that the data could not distinguish between the two specified orderings. Discussion The findings connect students’ perceived AI-related competencies and employment prospects with two distinguishable career cognitions: the salience of a desired occupational self and psychological openness to career boundaries. Their joint examination provides a differentiated account of concurrent associations in students’ career preparation. The cross-sectional findings do not establish causality, temporal precedence, or an underlying psychological sequence. Longitudinal and multi-source research is needed to examine temporal relationships and determine whether these associations extend to demonstrated AI competencies, career behavior, and actual employment outcomes.

item.title: Generative AI configurations across creative phases: a 2 × 2 experiment on creative performance and immediate knowledge in art and design education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in art and design education, but it remains unclear whether text-based and image-generative configurations offer different advantages across creative phases or whether sequencing them improves final outcomes. Methods In a randomized 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment, 120 art and design students (30 per condition) completed a standardized cultural-heritage chromatic reconstruction task. Participants were assigned to Text-to-Text, Text-to-Image, Image-to-Text, or Image-to-Image configurations across divergent exploration and convergent development. Expert-rated creative performance, immediate task-relevant knowledge, and human–AI interaction processes were assessed. The four primary hypothesis tests were evaluated with Holm correction. Results Text-based AI during divergence produced higher divergent creative performance than image-generative AI (mean difference = 0.823, Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Image-generative AI during convergence yielded higher Aesthetic Quality at the unadjusted level (difference = 0.493, p = 0.026), but not after Holm correction (adjusted p = 0.052). The hypothesized Text-to-Image sequence did not significantly outperform alternatives in Overall Creative Performance (contrast = 0.066, p = 0.671), and the factorial interaction was nonsignificant ( p = 0.541). However, Text-to-Image achieved higher baseline-adjusted immediate post-task knowledge scores (contrast = 1.478, 95% CI [1.050, 1.906], p < 0.001), without a significant cross-phase interaction ( p = 0.404). Discussion GenAI configuration effects differed across creative phases and outcomes, but phase-specific advantages did not establish a superior final creative-product sequence. Because AI modality was bundled with interaction and interface characteristics, and the knowledge assessments had limited reliability, the results do not establish isolated modality effects, durable learning, or synergistic sequencing. AI orchestration should remain a provisional, context-sensitive instructional perspective requiring further validation.

item.title: Latent profiles of social-media-specific and general appearance-related characteristics and body-related outcomes
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Appearance-related social media use has been associated with body dissatisfaction and eating-related concerns; however, most studies have employed variable-centred approaches, providing limited insight into how social-media-specific behaviours and broader appearance-related cognitive tendencies co-occur within individuals. Using a person-centred approach, we identified latent profiles defined by social-media content exposure, presentation and validation behaviours, upward appearance comparison, and body surveillance, and examined their concurrent associations with body-related outcomes. Methods A total of 3,504 Greek-speaking adults (66.8% women, mean age = 36.87 years, SD = 10.93) completed a cross-sectional online survey. Latent profile analysis used eight standardised indicators. Distal outcomes were examined using the Bolck -Croon -Hagenaars (BCH) three-step approach, accounting for classification uncertainty and adjusting for age, gender, and body mass index (BMI). Results The analysis supported six profiles: Photo-Manipulation -Focused Users (11.4%), Comparison and Surveillance -Focused Users (16.6%), Exposure-Dominant Users (22.5%), High Appearance-Engagement Users (3.6%), Moderate Appearance-Monitoring Users (24.4%), and Low Appearance-Engagement Users (21.5%). Classification precision was moderate (entropy = 0.710). Profiles differed in appearance satisfaction, drive for thinness, and self-compassion (all p < 0.001). The High Appearance-Engagement profile showed the highest drive for thinness and the lowest self-compassion and, together with the Comparison and Surveillance -Focused profile, the lowest appearance satisfaction. The Low Appearance-Engagement profile showed the lowest drive for thinness and, together with the Exposure-Dominant profile, the highest appearance satisfaction and self-compassion, despite the latter’s elevated exposure. Differences in all three outcomes remained, although attenuated, when profiles were derived from social-media-specific indicators alone. Discussion These findings indicate that distinct configurations of social-media behaviours and appearance-related cognitions are associated with differing body-related outcomes, reflecting heterogeneity that variable-centred analyses may obscure; longitudinal and experimental research is needed to establish temporal and causal relations.

item.title: Examining AI interaction profiles in generative AI supported fraction division problem posing
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new opportunities for mathematical problem posing, yet its relationship with the conceptual quality of posed problems and learners’ interaction profiles remains insufficiently understood. This study examines pre-service mathematics teachers’ fraction-division problem posing with and without GenAI support. Methods Using a mixed-methods descriptive–relational design, 57 pre-service mathematics teachers first posed a fraction-division word problem independently and then posed or revised a second problem with Google Gemini support. Problems were assessed using a rubric addressing general-mathematical quality and content-specific meanings of fraction division. Qualitative analysis of AI interactions identified three profiles: AI-Reliant, AI-Collaborative, and AI-Assistant. Quantitative analyses compared scores across phases and gains across profiles, incorporating robustness checks, multiple-comparison correction, effect sizes, and confidence intervals. Results AI-supported problems received significantly higher scores for contextual richness, language clarity, and content-specific meaning use; these differences remained significant after Holm correction. Problem type and solvability did not differ significantly. All participants retained the fraction-division meaning used in their independently posed problem, with changes consisting solely of added meanings, most often measurement division. Although AI-Assistant participants showed descriptively greater gains, differences across profiles were not statistically significant. Discussion The findings are consistent with refinement of representational and communicative features and more explicit articulation of existing fraction-division meanings, rather than correction of foundational mathematical understanding. The fixed-order design requires interpreting phase differences as associations rather than causal effects of GenAI. Small, unequal profile groups and wide confidence intervals also preclude interpreting nonsignificant differences as evidence of profile equivalence.

item.title: Changes in negative affect and resting-state EEG power following an EEG-derived generative reality art experience: a pilot pre–post study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Physiological signals are increasingly incorporated into personalized immersive media, but little is known about affective and neurophysiological changes when such signals are used as artistic material. This exploratory pilot study examined an electroencephalography (EEG)-derived generative virtual reality (VR) art experience in which participant-specific EEG signals were symbolically transformed into prompts for immersive visual environments. Thirty healthy university students completed the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule and resting-state EEG recordings before and after a single 5-min experience. EEG analyses examined log-transformed absolute alpha- and beta-band power across frontal, frontocentral, and central regions, with false discovery rate correction. Negative affect decreased from pre- to post-experience (mean change = −3.13, FDR-adjusted p = 0.004), whereas positive affect did not change significantly. Absolute beta-band power decreased across all three regions, and absolute alpha-band power decreased in the frontocentral and central regions (FDR-adjusted p values ≤0.022). Exploratory relative-power analyses showed no significant pre–post differences after correction for multiple comparisons. Frontal alpha asymmetry did not change significantly. Changes in EEG measures were not significantly associated with changes in affect after correction for multiple comparisons. The EEG findings therefore do not establish a neural mechanism for the reduction in negative affect. These findings indicate that the experience was associated with short-term changes in negative affect and resting-state spectral power. Because this pilot study used a single-group design, the findings do not establish causality or therapeutic efficacy. Instead, they provide an initial empirical basis for controlled research on physiological data as personalized material for immersive art and affective experience.

item.title: Career-related psychological cognitions and career exploration behavior among Chinese college students: statistical indirect pathways through generative artificial intelligence use
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence is changing how college students access career information, understand career opportunities, and prepare for job searching. Drawing on Social Cognitive Career Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model, this study used cross-sectional survey data to examine the relationships among career-related psychological cognitions, generative AI use, and career exploration behavior, and to test statistical indirect relationships through generative AI use. The sample consisted of 1,445 upper-year undergraduates from five universities in eastern China. Confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling, and bootstrap analyses were conducted. In the primary model, career self-efficacy and perceived usefulness of generative AI were significantly and positively associated with both generative AI use and career exploration behavior, and generative AI use was also significantly and positively associated with career exploration behavior. The path from career self-efficacy to generative AI use was statistically significant but small ( β = 0.082), as was the corresponding statistical indirect relationship with career exploration behavior; neither was significant in the Sample B-only sensitivity analysis. Perceived usefulness of generative AI showed a significant statistical indirect relationship with career exploration behavior through generative AI use in the primary model. Career insecurity showed a weak but significant positive bivariate correlation with generative AI use ( r = 0.095, p < 0.001); however, after career self-efficacy and perceived usefulness of generative AI were included simultaneously in the structural model, the path from career insecurity to generative AI use was close to zero and nonsignificant ( β = 0.000, p = 0.989). Career insecurity showed neither a significant structural path to career exploration behavior nor a significant statistical indirect relationship with it through generative AI use. Overall, the findings indicate that career self-efficacy and perceived usefulness of generative AI were associated with career exploration behavior in the primary model, whereas career insecurity did not show a significant independent structural path after the other predictors were considered simultaneously. Because the data were cross-sectional and self-reported, the indirect relationships should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than evidence of causal relationships.

item.title: Extension-semantic prompting for AI-generated traditional Chinese patterns: behavioral and semantic-aesthetic evaluation with exploratory fNIRS analysis
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background This study developed the Extension-Semantic Prompting Framework (ESPF) to organize cultural-semantic information in prompts for AI-generated traditional Chinese patterns. The framework decomposes traditional patterns into seven semantic-aesthetic dimensions and maps them onto structured prompt slots and corresponding evaluation items. Methods The experiment included 18 experts and 18 laypeople as participants. Stimuli comprised images of five traditional pattern themes generated using Stable Diffusion and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) models under the ESPF and Free conditions. Liking ratings, response times (RTs), and semantic-aesthetic questionnaire responses were analyzed using cross-classified mixed-effects models, while prefrontal functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) data were examined using region-of-interest (ROI) and general linear model analyses. Results Mixed-effects analyses showed that the ESPF condition was associated with shorter aesthetic-judgment RTs and higher framework-derived semantic-aesthetic ratings, although the latter varied significantly across pattern themes. Interpretation of the RT difference is limited by the fixed Free–ESPF presentation order. The overall condition effect on liking was not significant after accounting for participant and image variability. No stable condition-related effect was observed in the prefrontal ROIs, and exploratory between-group neural differences were not robust across adjusted and GLM analyses. Conclusion ESPF provides a structured approach to organizing cultural semantics in AI-generated traditional patterns. The selective differences observed across evaluation outcomes and pattern themes highlight the need to balance semantic control with creative openness in prompt-supported human–AI collaborative design.

item.title: Older adults’ social responses to AI virtual humans in digital kinship contexts: associations of loneliness, perceived cues and appraisals with purchase intention
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
As AI virtual humans become increasingly prominent communicative actors on short-video platforms, digital kinship content characterized by kinship-based forms of address, family narratives, caring expressions, and companionship-oriented interaction has begun to enter older adults’ everyday media use and become intertwined with commercial recommendation. Selectively drawing on the three-factor theory of anthropomorphism and integrating it with the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, this study conceptualizes loneliness as a manifestation of sociality motivation; emotional appeal, human likeness, and homophily as perceived cues and appraisals associated with elicited agent knowledge; and social presence and empathy as proximal social responses within the CASA framework. It examines older adults’ social perceptions of and emotional responses to kinship-oriented AI virtual humans and their associations with purchase intention. Using a standardized set of AI virtual human short videos representing key features of digital kinship content as stimuli, we collected valid data from 372 Chinese adults aged 65 years and older and employed partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) as parallel and complementary analytical approaches. The PLS-SEM results revealed distinct antecedent patterns for the two proximal responses. Emotional appeal showed the strongest association with social presence, whereas homophily was more strongly associated with empathy than with social presence. Human likeness was significantly associated only with social presence, while loneliness was positively associated with both responses. Empathy showed a stronger association with purchase intention than social presence, and all indirect associations were significant except the pathway from human likeness through empathy. The fsQCA results further showed that the combination of emotional appeal and empathy constituted the most stable configuration associated with high purchase intention, whereas loneliness emerged as a core condition only when homophily was also present. This study provides empirical evidence for understanding perceptions of social presence and empathy in later-life human–AI relational perception and offers practical implications for the governance of kinship-oriented AI commercial content and the protection of older consumers.

item.title: Design and Evaluation of an Immersive VR Space Based on Pedagogical Agent for Theory of Mind Training in Autistic Children: Insights from Brain Activity and Participatory Study
item.description:
Journal of Educational Computing Research
Virtual reality (VR) is widely recognized as a promising tool for social intervention in children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) However, it remains unclear how the design of virtual social partners shown in VR systems is optimized for the neural and behavioral responses in young children with ASD. The implementation pathway and intervention effects of VR spaces also need validation through empirical research. This study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining neural imaging experiment, qualitative inquiry, and participatory design to develop an immersive VR intervention space. Twenty-two autistic children (aged 3-8) completed theory of mind (ToM) tasks with virtual characters varying in anthropomorphism and interaction complexity. Neural activation was measured in brain regions related to mentalizing. Stakeholder preferences were gathered via interviews with clinical experts and collage workshops with autistic children. Results showed that virtual characters with rich interaction and low anthropomorphism elicited greater neural responses in children with ASD. Participatory design revealed children’s preferences for cartoon-style characters with expressive voices, simple verbal expressions, moderate facial expressions, and muted colors. A VR intervention space was designed and developed. Therapists reported a high score of usability, and caregivers reported improvements in children’s social skills. This study is the first to combine neuroimaging evidences with stakeholder-informed participatory design workshops to investigate autistic children’s preferences for virtual characters, and thereby design optimized VR-based intervention system. The interventional effectiveness was proved by both clinical experts and long-term training. This study provides theoretical and practical guidance for designing VR-based social interventions for autistic children.

item.title: Interactions between students and ChatGPT when solving a task on real functions: an exploratory analysis
item.description:
Technology Pedagogy and Education
Framed within the Theory of Mathematical Working Space, this exploratory study analysed the types of mathematical activities displayed by university students when formulating questions and requests to ChatGPT to solve a task involving real functions. To achieve this, the students’ personal working space that emerged from these interactions was characterised. The methodology was qualitative and interpretative, based on analysing the types of questions and requests addressed by the students to ChatGPT. A typology of questions was constructed, linked to the discovery, communication and reasoning planes, and an implicative analysis was applied to identify functional patterns. The results indicated that ChatGPT acted as a didactic artefact that reorganised students’ mathematical work, promoting processes of exploration, validation and argumentation. Among the conclusions, the study contributes to the understanding of the use of generative technologies in mathematics education.

item.title: Hybrid Human-AI Creativity: Navigating the Affordance Landscape of Creative Exploration
item.description:
Creativity Research Journal
The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems capable of producing text, images, music, and design artifacts has intensified debates about the nature of creativity and the locus of creative agency. Current discussions often frame these technologies either as replacing human creativity or as merely augmenting human creative processes. Such perspectives remain theoretically limited because they conceptualize creativity primarily as an individual cognitive ability rather than a distributed process embedded within sociocultural and material environments. Drawing on ecological approaches to cognition and contemporary creativity research, this paper proposes a conceptual framework that reconceptualizes human-AI creativity as navigation within an expanded affordance landscape. Integrating classical creativity process models with sociocultural and distributed perspectives, GenAI systems are conceptualized as affordance-modulating artifacts that reshape the topology of creative exploration. The framework explains how generative systems expand ideational possibility through rapid combinatorial generation while also influencing creative trajectories through algorithmic anchoring. Eight theoretical propositions link AI-mediated affordances to stages of the creative process. The paper extends distributed creativity theory to technologically mediated environments and outlines a research agenda for empirically investigating hybrid human-AI creativity systems.

item.title: Information ethics education and artificial intelligence ethical judgment among university students
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become an everyday study tool for university students, and how students judge its acceptable academic use is now an explicit target of educational policy. This cluster-randomized experiment tested whether an information ethics education module improves university students’ AI ethical judgment, whether improvements persist over four weeks, and whether effects depend on students’ daily generative AI use. Sixteen intact classes from three universities in Zhengzhou, China, were randomly assigned at the class level to a four-week information ethics education module (eight classes, n = 120) or to regular coursework (eight classes, n = 120). AI ethical judgment was measured before the module, immediately afterward, and four weeks later with a double-rated dilemma test covering six academic scenarios and three dimensions (ethical sensitivity, evaluative judgment, behavioral intention); inter-rater ICC(2,1) values were 0.897, 0.923, and 0.930 at the three waves. The design-consistent primary analysis, a multilevel model with random intercepts for students and classes, yielded a significant arm by wave interaction, χ 2 (2) = 60.94, p < 0.001: composite judgment rose in the intervention arm and did not change in the control arm. Cluster-robust and wild cluster bootstrap analyses supported the immediate effect (b = 0.354, cluster-robust SE = 0.065; bootstrap 95% CI [0.140, 0.566]) and the delayed effect (b = 0.225, SE = 0.061; bootstrap 95% CI [0.062, 0.386]). Four weeks later, 59.9% of the immediate gain was retained in the intervention arm and 63.4% of the between-arm effect, estimates consistent with partial retention given their wide intervals. The intervention effect was larger among students who used generative AI more frequently (interaction b = 0.206, cluster-robust p = 0.040). A short, curriculum-embedded information ethics module thus improved university students’ AI ethical judgment, with gains partially retained after four weeks and the largest benefits among frequent users.

item.title: Negotiating epistemic authority in AI-assisted lesson planning: a multiple-case study of preservice mathematics teachers
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can provide preservice teachers with a complete lesson plan before they have articulated the reasoning the plan is intended to develop, creating conditions for automation bias and cognitive offloading. This multiple-case study examined how five preservice mathematics teachers in China negotiated epistemic authority while planning using GenAI. Methods Cases were selected from 42 preservice teachers through preliminary quantitative screening. Screen-recording-derived event logs, concurrent verbalizations, video-stimulated recall interviews, and written reflections were integrated into an evidence matrix comprising 34 decision episodes. Authority was interpreted as retained, shared, or ceded based on the relationship among the source of a proposal, the participant’s action, the warrant invoked, and whether that warrant was enacted in the lesson plan. Results Authority was retained in 16 episodes, shared in 12, and ceded in 6, with variation across cases. Visible actions did not map onto authority positions in a fixed way, and professional warrants were sometimes not enacted. Two vulnerabilities emerged. A closed verification loop, observed in four episodes across two cases, occurred when participants recognized uncertainty about AI output yet asked the same AI to validate it. An insight–action gap, illustrated by three episodes in a single case, occurred when recognized pedagogica problems were not translated into planned teacher responses. Discussion The findings support the proposition that the educative value of AI-assisted planning depends less on how much novices edit AI output than on whether tasks require independent verification and warranted, enacted decisions.

item.title: Mapping digital health intervention components to Bandura’s sources of self-efficacy in cancer care: a scoping review
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Digital health technologies are increasingly used for symptom management, patient education, and continuity of care among people with cancer. However, the relationship between intervention components and theoretical pathways of self-efficacy has not been systematically mapped. Objective This scoping review aimed to describe the types, functional components, implementation characteristics, and self-efficacy outcome directions of digital health technologies designed to support self-efficacy in adults with cancer, and to map these components to Bandura’s sources of self-efficacy information. Methods This scoping review was conducted in accordance with the JBI methodological guidance and reported according to PRISMA-ScR. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library, and PsycINFO were searched from inception to January 9, 2026. Studies of digital health interventions for adult patients with cancer that reported self-efficacy outcomes were eligible. Two reviewers independently performed study selection, data extraction, and theory-based coding. Findings were synthesized using descriptive statistics, narrative synthesis, and evidence matrices. Results Twenty-one studies were included. Digital health technologies mainly included mobile applications, online platforms or websites, telehealth-supported care, and wearable devices; some studies integrated artificial intelligence, virtual simulation, text messaging, or other electronic communication tools. Intervention components included health education, self-monitoring, goal setting, task practice, feedback, professional support, peer interaction, reminders, and emotion regulation. Five studies reported significant improvement in overall self-efficacy, three reported improvement in specific dimensions, two reported improvement in high-engagement or subgroup analyses, three showed non-significant positive trends, and eight observed no significant change. In the descriptive comparison, moderate-to-strong mastery-experience coding was observed in all 10 studies reporting statistically significant improvement in overall, domain-specific, or high-engagement/subgroup self-efficacy, compared with 7 of 11 studies not reporting statistically significant improvement. Moderate-to-strong verbal-persuasion coding was observed in 10 of 10 and 6 of 11 studies, respectively. These patterns reflected co-occurrence rather than independent effects. Conclusion Digital health interventions varied substantially in functional components, theoretical operationalization, professional support, engagement, and outcomes. Moderate-to-strong mastery-experience and verbal-persuasion coding was more common among studies reporting statistically significant improvement. Future studies should report intervention components, theoretical pathways, engagement, professional support, and follow-up more consistently.

item.title: From “usefulness” to “dependence”: the dynamic evolution mechanism of generative AI use behaviors
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) rapidly permeates Chinese higher education, university students’ AI use behaviors have come to be characterized by “high frequency, wide penetration, and rapid iteration.” Yet, a systematic understanding of the dynamic evolution mechanism from initial cognition to deep dependence remains lacking. Methods Employing a four-wave longitudinal design spanning 18 months (the first week of June 2024 to the first week of December 2025, with one wave every 6 months) and drawing on 524 valid responses to the 600 distributed questionnaires, retained in full across all four waves, this study systematically investigates the dynamic trajectories and mediating mechanisms of 12 core constructs, including perceived usefulness, trust, technology concerns, ethical concerns, use behavior, technology integration, usage habits, academic dependence, and moral disengagement. Results Repeated-measures ANOVA and mediation model testing reveal the following: (1) Perceived usefulness exhibits an asymmetric U-shaped trajectory of “sharp initial decline, stabilization, and rebound,” which does not support the hypothesized inverted U-shaped pattern. (2) Trust shows a trajectory of “adjusted decline, low-level stabilization, and internalized overshooting,” with an “overshooting” phenomenon in the later stage that surpasses the initial level. (3) Technology concerns decrease in a strictly monotonic fashion, whereas ethical concerns follow an asymmetric U-shaped trajectory of “precipitous decline, stabilization, and sharp rebound,” revealing a differentiated pattern of technological desensitization and ethical re-sensitization. (4) Technology integration partially mediates the transformation from actual use behavior to usage habits (indirect effect proportion = 23.39%), with the cognitive pathway accounting for only about one-quarter of the total association. (5) Early trust significantly and positively predicts continuance intention 18 months later (β = 0.400), and this effect is partially mediated by user satisfaction. (6) Exploratory analyses show that perceived usefulness negatively predicts academic dependence and moral disengagement through the sequential mediation of “actual use behavior → technology integration → usage habits,” suggesting that “high usefulness” may lead to benign autonomous use rather than problematic dependence. Conclusion This study is among the first to adopt a longitudinal design to reveal the nonlinear dynamic evolution patterns of GenAI use behaviors among Chinese university students. It provides crucial empirical evidence for extending technology acceptance theories along the temporal dimension, for understanding the stratified evolution of risk perception, and for informing AI education interventions. The sample was recruited by convenience sampling and consists almost entirely of female students in the humanities and social sciences; the findings describe this sample, and no claim of generalization to all Chinese university students is made.

item.title: Neuroergonomic Comparison of User Experience and System Performance for SSVEP-Based Brain Computer Interfaces in Mixed Reality and Virtual Reality Environments
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Steady-state visual evoked potential (SSVEP)-based brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) deliver high classification accuracy and information transfer rates (ITR), yet their neural responses and user experience vary across immersive display environments. This study compares SSVEP signal characteristics, offline decoding performance, and subjective experience between mixed reality (MR) and virtual reality (VR) head-mounted display (HMD) setups to inform ecologically valid real-world BCI paradigms. Identical visual flicker stimuli (10, 11.25, 15, 18 Hz) were presented via Apple Vision Pro under MR and VR modes. Nine occipito - parietal electroencephalogram (EEG) channels were processed with filter bank canonical correlation analysis (FBCCA) to calculate signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), offline classification accuracy (ACC), and ITR. Subjective workload and immersive experience were quantified using the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) and a customized motion-sickness questionnaire. No statistically significant inter-group difference in grand-averaged SSVEP SNR was detected between MR and VR (F (1,20) = 1.002, p = 0.329). Numerically higher ACC and ITR values were observed for MR (19.51 vs. 18.57 bits/min), but these performance gaps did not reach statistical significance. In exploratory paired comparisons, MR showed lower directional imbalance scores and higher game-experience scores (Z = − 3.431, p = 0.001, r = − 0.75). Across both environments, low-frequency flicker (10, 11.25 Hz) elicited significantly stronger SSVEP responses than high-frequency stimuli (15, 18 Hz, p < 0.001). MR generates consistent SSVEP neural signals alongside favorable subjective perceptual experience, with only non-significant numerical gains in offline decoding efficiency. Key limitations of this work include a small young-adult sample, exclusive offline signal analysis without closed-loop online validation, and inherent optical confounds from differing MR/VR rendering luminance and contrast. These findings provide preliminary offline evidence supporting MR’s usability for home-based rehabilitation and smart-environment BCI applications, while larger-scale online experiments are required to confirm its objective decoding benefits.

item.title: From generation to judgment: the multidimensional structure of design thinking mindset and differences across learning stages in AIGC-supported fashion film design learning
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) is changing how design alternatives are generated in fashion film design learning, enabling students to obtain large numbers of comparable and iteratively refinable visual outcomes within a short period. However, expanded generative capacity does not, by itself, determine how learners interpret, evaluate, experiment with, and select among uncertain outcomes. In this human–AI collaborative creative environment, empirical evidence remains limited on whether learners’ design-related psychological tendencies form a distinguishable multidimensional structure that is comparable across learning stages. Design Thinking Mindset (DTM) provides a multidimensional psychological framework for addressing this issue. Methods Drawing on Vignoli et al.’s DTM framework, this study examined five dimensions—Uncertainty and Risk, Empathy, Experimentation, Abductive Reasoning, and Creative Confidence—through a cross-sectional survey of 409 first-year and third-year students from three Chinese universities who had experience with AIGC fashion film design projects. Confirmatory factor analysis and measurement invariance testing across year groups were used to examine the five-dimensional structure and its measurement comparability, followed by latent mean comparisons. Results The five DTM dimensions formed a correlated yet distinguishable structure and demonstrated measurement comparability across year groups. Third-year students had significantly higher latent means on all five dimensions, with the largest descriptive standardized difference point estimates observed for Abductive Reasoning and Creative Confidence. Discussion These findings provide empirical support for the applicability of five selected DTM dimensions in AIGC-supported fashion film design learning and reveal distinct patterns of self-reported psychological tendencies across year groups. From an educational perspective, the results suggest that AIGC-supported design education should attend not only to the generation of creative alternatives but also to learners’ psychological orientations toward uncertainty, experimentation, audience understanding, creative reasoning, and confidence in creative work.

item.title: Generative AI dependency and perceived learning outcomes among university students: an indirect association involving effort regulation
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into university learning, raising questions about dependency-oriented reliance and self-regulation. Drawing on a self-regulated learning perspective, this study examined associations among GenAI dependency, effort regulation, and multidimensional perceived learning outcomes, including the statistical indirect association involving effort regulation. Methods Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 982 students at three higher education institutions in Guangdong Province, China. Confirmatory factor analysis and covariance-based structural equation modeling were conducted, with indirect associations tested using 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for GenAI use frequency. Results The measurement model showed acceptable fit (CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.043, SRMR = 0.041). GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = −0.087) and was negatively associated with effort regulation ( β = −0.257). Effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.497). The residual direct association was nonsignificant ( β = 0.041), whereas the indirect association was negative and significant ( β = −0.128). After adjustment for GenAI use frequency, the indirect association remained significant, but the small total association was no longer significant. Conclusion The findings highlight effort regulation as a relevant learner-controlled process in the association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. They also distinguish dependency-oriented reliance from frequency of GenAI use. The cross-sectional design and potential classroom clustering warrant cautious interpretation.

item.title: Screening-positive subclinical eating disorder symptoms and associated factors among high school students: a cross-sectional study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Subclinical eating disorder (SCED) symptoms are common among adolescents and may be associated with adverse psychological and behavioral outcomes. However, evidence on screening-positive SCED symptoms and associated factors among high school students remains limited. Identifying these factors may support early screening and prevention. Methods In December 2023, a stratified random cluster sampling method was used to recruit students from 12 high schools in Yangzhou, Jiangsu Province, China. Data were collected using a self-developed general information questionnaire, the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire 6.0 (EDE-Q 6.0), the Ma Body Figure Scale, the Children’s Depression Inventory–Short Form (CDI-S), the Spence Children’s Anxiety Scale–Short Version (SCAS-S), the National Mental Health Literacy Questionnaire, and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. BMI was classified using the WHO 2007 age- and sex-specific BMI-for-age reference for participants younger than 19 years, with adult WHO BMI cut-offs used for participants aged 19 years or older. Generalized estimating equations (GEE) with school as the clustering variable were used to examine factors associated with screening-positive SCED symptoms. Results A total of 2,681 high school students were included in the analysis, of whom 645 (24.1%) screened positive for SCED symptoms. In the school-clustered GEE model, female sex (OR = 1.351, 95% CI: 1.109–1.645), overweight (OR = 3.418, 95% CI: 2.632–4.439), obesity (OR = 7.740, 95% CI: 5.939–10.089), positive body image misperception (OR = 4.280, 95% CI: 3.533–5.184), higher depressive symptom scores (OR per 1-SD increase = 1.454, 95% CI: 1.297–1.630), higher anxiety symptom scores (OR per 1-SD increase = 1.387, 95% CI: 1.269–1.516), and poor sleep quality (OR = 1.393, 95% CI: 1.121–1.733) were associated with higher odds of screening-positive SCED symptoms. Adequate mental health literacy was associated with lower odds (OR = 0.609, 95% CI: 0.506–0.734). Conclusion Approximately one-quarter of the participating high school students screened positive for SCED symptoms. Screening-positive SCED symptoms were associated with weight status, body image misperception, depressive and anxiety symptom severity, sleep quality, and mental health literacy. These findings support multidimensional school-based screening and health education while recognizing that the EDE-Q threshold identifies a screening-defined condition rather than a clinical diagnosis.

item.title: Perceived AI literacy and TPACK in pre-service teacher education: mediating roles of perceived usefulness, ease of use, and value in blended learning
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into blended learning requires pre-service teachers to develop AI-related competencies and the ability to integrate technology into pedagogy. This study examines how perceived AI literacy and technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) are associated with deep learning through perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and perceived value of AI use. Methods A cross-sectional survey was completed by 423 pre-service teachers enrolled in blended learning courses at a university in China. Data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), with covariance-based structural equation modeling and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) used as complementary robustness and configurational analyses. Results Perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and perceived value of AI use significantly mediated the relationships between the two competencies and deep learning. All six indirect pathways were significant in both the PLS-SEM and covariance-based SEM analyses. The fsQCA revealed an equifinal and asymmetric structure: multiple, partly substitutable conditions were sufficient for high deep learning, and no single condition was necessary for either high or low deep learning. Conclusions The findings integrate the technology acceptance model and expectancy-value theory to explain how pre-service teachers' competencies and perceptions relate to deep learning in AI-enhanced blended environments. Teacher education should support technical competence alongside positive perceptions of AI's utility, usability, and value. Because the measures were self-reported and collected cross-sectionally at one university, the findings are interpreted as associational and configurational rather than causal.

item.title: Teachers’ basic psychological need satisfactions and their intentions to use generative artificial intelligence: the mediating role of engagement in professional development
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers new opportunities for instructional innovation, yet the psychological mechanisms underlying teachers’ intentions to adopt it remain unclear. Intrinsic motivation is an important internal factor shaping teachers’ intentions to use GenAI and is closely linked to the satisfaction of their basic psychological needs. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), this study develops and tests a theoretical framework linking teachers’ basic psychological need satisfaction to their intention to use GenAI through intrinsic motivation and engagement in professional development. Such engagement may foster innovation in GenAI-supported teaching practices. Methods Survey data were collected from 146 teachers participating in a GenAI learning program. Structural equation modeling was used to examine the hypothesized relationships among basic psychological need satisfaction, intrinsic motivation, engagement in professional development, and intention to use GenAI. Results Perceived competence in using GenAI was significantly and positively associated with intrinsic motivation, whereas perceived autonomy and relatedness were not significantly associated with intrinsic motivation. Engagement in professional development mediated the relationship between intrinsic motivation and intention to use GenAI. Discussion These findings provide a nuanced understanding of the psychological mechanisms underlying teachers’ intentions to adopt GenAI, highlighting the roles of perceived competence, intrinsic motivation, and engagement in professional development. They also offer practical implications for supporting the integration of GenAI into teaching.

item.title: Teachers’ attitudes and behavioural intentions towards AI integration in Chinese higher education: a qualitative interview study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction The rapid expansion of generative AI has intensified scholarly and policy debate over its role in higher education, yet university teachers’ attitudes towards its integration remain complex and context-dependent. This study explores how university teachers perceive, experience, and respond to AI integration in their teaching. Guided primarily by the three-component attitude model and informed by the technology acceptance model and the theory of planned behaviour, the study examines cognitive appraisals, affective responses, behavioural intentions, and perceived support needs. Methods The study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 university teachers from four higher education institutions in China. The interview data were analysed using codebook-informed thematic analysis combining deductive and inductive coding. Results The findings indicate that teachers generally perceive AI as a supportive rather than substitutive educational tool, valuing it for improving efficiency, supporting lesson preparation, and enriching pedagogical design. Emotional responses varied from enthusiasm and a sense of accomplishment to caution, neutrality, and, in some cases, declining satisfaction. Across the interviews, teachers’ primary concerns centred less on their own replacement than on the perceived risks of inappropriate AI use for students’ independent thinking, reasoning, originality, and authentic understanding. Teachers’ intentions to adopt AI were therefore conditional and bounded, shaped by pedagogical purpose, disciplinary context, student readiness, and the need to maintain teacher control. Teachers also emphasised that sustainable AI integration requires more than general encouragement, calling instead for AI literacy development, discipline-sensitive support, specialised tools, and enabling institutional infrastructure. Discussion Overall, these findings extend contextual understandings of teachers’ AI acceptance by showing how adoption intentions are pedagogically negotiated and highlight the importance of supporting professional judgement and students’ independent thinking in higher education.

item.title: Human-in-the-loop semantic learning analytics for assessing moral-value reasoning in university AI ethics education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction University AI ethics education addresses fairness, privacy, accountability, transparency, human autonomy, and academic integrity, but the semantic structure of students' moral-value reasoning and its connection to responsible solutions remain insufficiently characterized. This study examined a human-in-the-loop semantic learning analytics framework for task-specific moral-value reasoning. Methods Ninety science and engineering graduate students completed an online explicit-reflective AI ethics module in a one-group pre–post multimethod study without a control group. Assessments comprised an AI ethics knowledge test, a perceived-awareness scale, and open-ended ethical reasoning tasks. Expert annotations informed transformer-based multi-label coding, descriptive value coverage and balance metrics, problem–solution coupling, and baseline-only nested cross-validated prediction of subsequent raw problem-solving change. Results Within-participant pre–post increases were observed in ethical knowledge, perceived moral-value awareness, actual ethical awareness, problem–solving skills, value coverage, value balance, and problem–solution coupling. Automated semantic coding achieved participant-grouped cross-validated macro-F1 = 0.83 (95% CI [0.78, 0.87]; micro-F1 = 0.86; macro-AUPRC = 0.82). The baseline-only prediction model yielded cross-validated R 2 = 0.30 (95% CI [0.11, 0.45]) for subsequent raw problem-solving change. Discussion Expert-supervised semantic analytics can characterize value representation and issue–solution reasoning in AI ethics assessments. Coverage and balance describe response structure rather than moral quality. The absence of a control group, repeated use of one scenario, and modest sample size preclude causal and broad trait-level conclusions.

item.title: Uneven automation: comparing authorship anxiety and generative AI use among art and design undergraduate students
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Art and design education expects students to develop a sense of authorship over original work, but generative AI (GenAI) complicates how students understand and claim that authorship. This study examined whether these experiences differ across creative fields through a mixed-methods design. The survey included 2,441 GenAI-using students from seven field categories at 33 art and design institutions in China and assessed authorship anxiety, creative agency, perceived usefulness, dependence on GenAI, and frequency of use. The quantitative analysis first examined variation across all seven categories and then compared fine art with the five applied design fields. Interview data from 22 survey participants were also examined thematically. The main findings include that (1) authorship anxiety did not differ significantly across the seven categories or between fine art and pooled design; the latter comparison met the equivalence criterion at ±d = 0.20, but not at tighter bounds; (2) clearer differences emerged in how students used GenAI. Compared with fine-art students, design students considered GenAI more useful and used it more frequently; (3) across the interviews, most students described authorship as retaining control over the creative idea while delegating parts of its execution to GenAI. Specifically, fine-art students often grounded authorship in embodied making and human imperfection, whereas design students placed greater emphasis on judgement, selection, and control. We call this pattern uneven automation: concern about authorship was broadly shared, but students in different fields responded to GenAI in different ways, potentially reflecting the varying labour-market pressures surrounding their disciplines.

item.title: When thanks have nowhere to go: emotional indebtedness in the age of service robots
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction When hotel service robots deliver meaningful service, customers may experience emotional indebtedness—a moral-emotional state arising from perceived obligation without a clear target for reciprocity. This study examines how social (social presence, enjoyment) and nonsocial (novelty, performance) attributes of service robots influence emotional indebtedness and subsequent brand loyalty. Methods Survey data were collected from 462 hotel guests in China with direct service robot experience. Structural equation modeling (SEM) with maximum likelihood estimation was employed, incorporating second-order latent constructs and multi-group analysis by anthropomorphism level. Results Social attributes significantly increased emotional indebtedness, whereas nonsocial attributes either reduced or failed to elicit such responses. Emotional indebtedness positively predicted brand loyalty. Multi-group analyses revealed that the effect of social attributes on emotional indebtedness was invariant across anthropomorphism levels, whereas anthropomorphism moderated the relationship between nonsocial attributes and emotional indebtedness and the conversion of indebtedness into brand loyalty. Discussion These findings extend social exchange theory to robot-mediated hospitality services, demonstrating that customers’ moral-emotional responses depend more on how robot interactions are socially interpreted than on functional performance alone. Anthropomorphism functions as a selective boundary condition rather than a uniform amplifier of emotional engagement.

item.title: Low-dimensional burnout risk classification in engineering students: the role of demand-recovery interaction features
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Student burnout is a rapidly growing concern, with prior research linking its development to a wide range of psychological, behavioral, and contextual factors. Machine learning approaches have recently shown strong predictive performance for identifying burnout, but typically rely on high-dimensional datasets impractical for real-world use. Whether burnout can be reliably identified from a minimal set of variables remains underexplored. This study addresses that gap using a low-dimensional predictive framework in undergraduate engineering students. Grounded in Conservation of Resources theory, three classifiers (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) were evaluated across three feature configurations (Raw: all nine unengineered base predictors, including academic, demographic, sleep, and physical activity variables; Engineered: four demand–recovery interaction features; Full: Raw combined with Engineered) to test whether burnout reflects academic load alone or an imbalance between demand and recovery capacity. The Full configuration performed best: Logistic Regression and Random Forest exceeded a matched permutation-based null (Global MCC = 0.173 and 0.190, respectively, p < 0.05), while Gradient Boosting did not reach significance (MCC = 0.126, p = 0.066). Across 50 alternative fold splits, however, mean Global MCC for the Full configuration was lower for each classifier (Logistic Regression 0.09, Random Forest 0.16, Gradient Boosting 0.11), indicating that the primary-split estimates are upper-range. In addition, adding engineered features to Raw predictors did not produce a statistically distinguishable improvement in Global MCC for any classifier. Moderate Risk classification remained difficult across all classifiers and configurations, with most confidence intervals crossing zero. Permutation importance identified Workload-Sleep Strain as the most influential predictor in the Random Forest model, suggesting the engineered features capture meaningful behavioral patterns. However, because these variables are deterministic transformations of the raw predictors, their incremental contribution could not be confirmed statistically. These results offer preliminary evidence that a small set of sleep, activity, workload, and engineered variables carries predictive signal for burnout risk above chance.

item.title: The effect of moral evaluations on the intention to use human augmentation technology: moral considerations as a mediator of personal and societal adoption intentions
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Inroduction Human augmentation technologies (HAT) enhance human abilities through device-based integration or extension of the human body. Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) represent a versatile form of HAT, spanning motor, sensory, and cognitive augmentation across a spectrum from restoration to expansion. Although past research identified ethical evaluations as key determinants of HAT acceptance, it remains unclear whether moral evaluations mediate the relationship between technology and user characteristics and usage intentions. This paper examines whether the effects of augmentation-specific (type and purpose of augmentation) and user-specific (disability status) characteristics on personal and societal intention to use HAT are mediated by moral evaluations. Methods We conducted two online experimental vignette studies with German participants. Study 1 employed a 3 × 4 between-participants design ( N = 1,142) with text-based vignettes depicting BCIs varying in augmented ability type and augmentation purpose. Study 2 used video vignettes in a between-participants design ( N = 1,201) featuring workload-adaptive BCIs used by either disabled or able-bodied drivers. We assessed usage intentions via adapted TAM2 scales and moral evaluation via an adapted Multidimensional Ethics Scale. Results Path models show that the effects of augmentation type, augmentation purpose, and user status on personal usage intention were fully mediated by moral evaluations. For societal usage intention, models indicate that moral evaluations fully mediate the effects of augmentation characteristics, and partially mediate those of user status. Discussion These findings indicate that moral evaluations constitute one pathway linking augmentation and user characteristics to BCI acceptance. Overall, this study advances the understanding of ethical aspects in HAT acceptance, using BCIs as an example.
